He does, he would neuer haue left me els, he 〈◊〉 And now me thinks J loath him more then I lou'd him ▪ goe run for Hortenſio my guardian, bid him come armd, thet's intent of treaſon tell him. I wonder you dare come in my ſight, conſidering the wrong you did me. Tis too long and twere ſhorter then tis, will he not court me? not? no • ſpeak to me neither? nay neuer ask pardon ▪ tis to late, we ſhal ha'you come to my window one of theſe mornings with muſicke, but doe not, my patience is to much out of tune, out of my ſight I hate thee, worſe then I loath painting, I hate thee, out of my ſight. Ile kiſſe a toad firſt. you will. Out humourd? O I would ſell my part of immortality. O how ſpleene ſwells mee? helpe Hortenſio, creepe a my knees? Hotenſio. Do not kill him, though hee deſerues death yet doe not kill him, onely diſweapon him; ſo. I will not heare him, keepe him; but keepe him ſafe on your liues, if he get away or miſcarry in priſon: as I am heire of Venice ile haue your heads for't. they bind Fie, fie, with a cord? here, bind him with my ſcarfe, that wil hold, and yet ſtand away, ile doo't my ſelfe, I cannot truſt him with you, leaſt you ſhould let him ſometime ſcape free: beſides, you cannot vſe him according to the quality of his offence, and becauſe ile glory in his bondage my chamber ſhall bee his pri ſon, let him haue neither light meat nor drinke, but what J pro uide him my ſelfe. Oh you are not gone then. He would anger me. Should J haue let him go, (as I could no other way detaine him in modeſty) and he had ſet his loue on ſome other, t'would haue fretted my hart ſtrings a ſunder. Not for any hate, but in pride of my humour. That I may feede mine eie with the ſight of him, and be ſure no other beauty can rob me of his company: I will ha't all, I will not looſe an ynch of him: And in this, I but imitate our Ita lian dames, who cauſe their friends to clap their iealous huſbands in priſon, that if they haue occaſion to vſe them within fortie weekes and a day, they may ſurely know where to find them. Ile ſplit my heart ere my humor ſtrike ſaile: here comes his Page, how now boy? how doth your maſter. VVell? VVhere is he? Is he dead? My Aſpero dead! Boy See madam, what a mutation I ſee too much, and curſe my proud humour that was the cauſe of it: Aſpero, kind ſoule, proud ſullen Florimell, diſdainefull humor, that in one minute haſt eternally vndone me: I would not kiſſe the liuing ſubſtance, that being dead doate on thy picture: oh I lou'd thee euer with my ſoule: O let me kiſſe this ſhrowd of beauty: I would not accept thee liuing, that being dead on my knees adore thee: could kiſſes recouer thee, I would dwell on thy lips: kneele till my knees grew to the ground, deere gentle Aſpero ſhe that procurde thy death will die with thee, And craue no heauen, but ſtill to lie with thee. Liues Aſpero? Am I ore reacht? Do not flowt me; and you doe, I ſhall grow into my humour againe. In earneſt I ſhall, and then I know what I know. In ieaſt. No more, thou haſt driuen mee cleane out of conceite with my humor, I loue thee, I confeſſe it, ſhalt be my husband, ile liue with thee, thou art my life, and ile die with thee. VVhat more I meane is coated in my looke, If thou acceptſt it, ſweare, Boy, run to the maſter of my Gundelo, and will him attend me after ſupper at the garden ſtaires, I meane to take the euening ayre, tell him. Nay if I ſay the word, it ſhall be done Aſpero ▪ The foole comes without calling. As good ſay ſteale my Lord, what mary-bone of witte is your iudgement going to pick now? Treaſon? My roiall fathers: Can he be cloſer then in my cuſtody? And dare not you truſt mee? Do you obſerue how he flowts you my Lord? that I had bin his keeper but one night longer ▪ but keepe him cloſe, if he eſcape (though againſt thy will) as I am a mayd, Shalt pay as deere for't as thou didſt for thy office. I ſhall wiſh thee hangd, if he do not: treaſon! I may thanke my peeuiſh humor fort. Thou bringſt phyſicke when the patient's dead boy: out ieaſt's turnd earneſt. As good, or rather worſe, hee's buried quick. Hee's buried in cloſe priſon boy, hee's knowne for the duke of Mantuaes ſonne, and by my fathers letter a ••• ched for a traytor. The teſtie aſſe Hortenſio. We cannot. Shall he be couſend? Call out the iaylor boy, yet doe not; haſt got a beard like Hortenſio? VVouldſt rob him of his wit? Put it on boy. Very ill, and my plot worſe. I purpoſde, thou in the habit of Hortenſio, ſhouldſt vnder pretence of remouing Aſpero to a new priſon, haue freed him out of the old one. Prithee call him. VVhy how now gallant, not gone yet? VVeele haue you hangd out i'the freſh ayre, one of theſe mornings. Yes, when you had hangd abroad a little: but my Lorde Hortenſio (for I think I muſt be your Lady when all's done) what ſport? I would be merry a purpoſe to make him mad; the room's priuate and fit for any exerciſe. No, I loue ſome ſtirring exerciſe, my body's condiciond like the ſun; it would neuer be out of motion. At the happines of your wit my Lord, that you ſhoulde hit vpon that ſport, which of all other I delight in. Weele haue the thing it ſelfe firſt; and as we like that, weel heare your Apologie after: who ſhall be hud-winckt ſirſt? My ſcarfe, take my ſcarfe my Lord. Mary that will I my Lord, let me alone to blind you. But how if you take me? as I know that will be your ayme, An eaſie ranſome: ile not be priſoner long, if a kiſſe will en large me. Me thinks he looks for all the world like God Cupid. He cannot come to faſt, O I am taken priſoner. Is that your law of armes? My lips like faithfull Treaſurers ſhall ſee it diſchargde. Am I freed now? Here Aſpero, on with this beard and gowne: I thinke hee followes me by the ſent, his hat, ſo: a narrowe miſſe yfaith my Lord? Euen vpon going, one of you counterfet my voice, there I deceiud you my Lord. Not yet, but I will, and you look not the better too't, buſie him till you thinke we are out of the Court, and then followe vs: you ſhall find vs at the ſouth port, now or neuer my Lord. Peremptory iacke, iaylor, as you reſpect your office, lay ſpe ciall watch that none of what degree ſoeuer haue acceſſe to him. If he call for me, tell him I ſcorne him. But come not at him. But giue him none. He may fire the houſe, let him haue none. If he rayle, ſing. Do any thing to vexe him. Tis a ſigne they loue you ▪ Then you doe not loue the Commons. One that has playd the part of a Conſtable, brought you home a Runaway. And am I not a good child to leaue my fathers loue at ſixe and ſeauen, and hazard my honor vpon your ſonnes naked pro miſe, and your hopefull acceptance. Shall neretheleſſe retaine his ſimpathy, Anthonio know I am loues reſolute, Confirmd and grounded in affection: I lou'd your ſonne, not for he was a Prince, But one no better then his preſent fortunes, Ile loue him ſtill, ſince firſt I lou'd him ſo, Let Father, friends, and all the world ſay no. Why Ladies, haue you ſuch large intereſt in our brothers. They offer parlee, let mee anſwer them. Brothers, how now? who made you ſouldiers? Faith een my father as he made you louers ▪ What? hath he chang'd your ſhepheards hooks to ſwords? Of Amoradoes made you armed knights? O ſeld-ſeene metamorphoſis! J haue knowne Souldiers turne louers, but for amorous louers To re-aſſume their valour, tis a change, Like winter-thunder, and a thing as ſtrange. Free will, brothers, mine owne freewill, all free in Mantua, here's freewill yfaith, ſpeake am I not a free-woman? You lie boy. Shame? not a whit: but come, your wenches brothers, I make no queſtion, I haue won my wager: Are they as faire as I? By heauen, th'are villains all that thinke him ſo, I ſhould curſe my ſelfe if I ſhould hate him: Why boy it ſeemes they dare not, VVell done yfaith wenches, O that the olde gray-beard my Father were here, ide haue about with him as I am honoura ble. Looke, thinke, find, proue, doe what you can, Theſe are the wenches that you courted than: Then hony bees lay by your ſmarting ſtings, and buz ſweet loue into your Ladies eares, Tell them of kiſſes, and ſuch prety things, Theſe drumming dub adubs loues pleaſure feares. Fatherinfaith they will. One that I ſtumbled on at Blindman buffe, a proper man, a man euery ynch of him: and you would ſay ſo, and you knewe but aſmuch as I—meane to know ere I haue done with him ▪
speeches.Oct: Haue we not Padua Shalt be reuengd, giue me money, ile be thy ſnaile & ſcore out a ſiluer path to his confuſion.
True, ſhee's parcell Poet, parcell fidler already, and they commonly ſing three parts in one. This would haue done rare at a ſchollers window, How do you like it father? I do admire to heare my princely father thus mertilie diſcourſe of trifling loue. Indeed we will. Prithee what? Not to diſſemble, we haue. Indeed I am in loue to be in loue. But is it good in loue to be in doubt ▪ Your doubtfull counſell counſells vs to loue. Theſe are too meane for loue, brother lets leaue them. Though againſt ſtomack.— Tis well, if that well met we be to you. Ile ſay thy cheek no naturall beauty lacks, Peace doatard, peace, thy ſight of loue is done, Thou canſt not ſee the glory of loues ſunne. Spent age with froſty clowds thy ſight doth dim, That thou art blind to ſee and apt to ſin. Hinder not our way. Exennt brothers. Call you this ſorrowes caue? To what compare ſhall I compare thee to? Vncomparable beauties Paragon. O ſhe is faire. Both more faire Then rocks of pearle, or the chaſt euening ayre. Why where liues ſad griefe? heer's all ſpeaking ioy. Haue they bin faire? what fayrer then they are? VVhy tis not poſſible, this heauenly faire Hath only in it ſelfe beauties exceed, O then rich, fayre, and onely ſelues exceed. As 〈…〉
To pleaſe my Father, ile inqueſt of beauty, And neuer make returne till I haue found, A loue ſo faire, ſo rich, ſo honorable, As fits the honor of Octanioes ſonnes. Now ſirra what haue you been about? But your boyſhip hath ſo ſought vs, that wee haue found you. VVell ſir, no more, here comes our royall Father. Father ſuch coſt doth paſſe your ſons reuenues We take example from immortall Ioue, Who like a ſhepheard would repaire to loue. Ile gage a 100. crownes mine proues the faireſt. How if't be fowle? Oh ſtale, that ieaſt runs oth'lees. O ſhallow wit, at the bottome ſo ſoone. Is it not paſt two, doth it not come ſomewhat neere three ſiſter: They ſhall haue deeds. What canſt do: Canſt keepe counſell ▪ Then to doubt loue is the ne • t way to loue ▪ VVe did, we m • t • n kindred, we are brothers. Say we deſire to husband it with you. But will you truſt a ſhepheard when he vowes, Let vs perſwade you to beleeue we loue you. Brother the laſt is fayreſt in my eie. Firſt in your choice, but not in beauty ſir. No, but in loue. Yet they are faire: we loue, thou art loues foe. No neuer. Fie, fie, how heauy is light loue in me? This leaden ayre, This pondrous feather, merry Melancholy. And ſhapeleſſe loue Hath in his watch of loue oreſlept himſelfe. Nay then tis ſo, my heauenly loue's gone by, And ſtruck him dead with her loue-darting eye. Out Atheiſt, thou prophan ▪ ſt loues deity, For, falſe-reporter, I in them haue ſeene A loue that makes a Negro of Loues Queene: One that when as the ſunne keeps holliday, Hir beauty clads him in his beſt array, Jle ſay ſhe is like Cynthia when day's done, Or Lady to the miſtriſſe of the night. One ſmile would lay my iarring thoughts at reſt. Goddeſſe. VVhat time, ſweet loue, keepe fiſhes when they bite? VVhy? Come, th'art all enuy, feed vpon thy hate, This day our queſt of loue ſhall terminate. Feare not old man, he was the meanes that breath'd this ſpirit into vs. Not ſtand? it ſhall: not Iou • 〈…〉 the ground ▪ worke 〈◊〉 loue ▪ They haue our loues. Our hearts and hands. And not afore? Has not Anthonies ſonne Sent them by ſome baſe practiſe to their death? In act: Princeſſe, we haue, within there: reach our ſhields, When beauty fights, the God of battaile yeelds. Exeunt. Our ſiſter priſoner? J wag? are you there too? VVhy ſiſter, ſhame you not to ſet your loue On one, that is our Fathers enemie. We thinke thee a proud villain and our foe. Bring the ladders forth, Brauely aſſault to ſeparate their liues, As they are ſealing the walls, the Ladies come forth. VVhat nymphe or god deſſe in my Hermiaes ſhape, Stands to debar my entrance to the towne: Immortall Pallas that art more diuine, In my loues beautie that thou cloth'ſt thee in, With drawe thy ſelfe, and giue our fury limits. VVhats here! A ſhepheard wooing of a Country maide, As ſhe ſits angling by a Riuers ſide, By them an aged man making a net! The Motto ▪ Sic! this Emblems morrall is, The former loue I had with Lucida, And this hope tells me that's faire ▪ Lucida. The more I looke, the more me thinkes tis ſhe. VVhat ſhould I thinke to proue it is not ſhe? O heauen, oh fortune, and moſt happie ſtars, Do I find loue, where I expected wars? VVhy are we not in armes father. VVe lik'd them firſt.
Go daughters with your Angels to the brooke, And ſee if any ſiluer-coated fiſh, Will nibble at your worme-emboweldhooks: Decciue the wat • y ſubiects, yet the name Of foule deceit me thinks ſhould fray them from you, Alack, alack, I cannot blame the world, That in the world there is ſo much deceipt; When this poore ſimple trade muſt vſe deceipt. But with what conſcience can J make this net, Within whoſe meſhes all are caught that come: They couſen one at once, this couſens many, I will vndoo't it ſhall not couſen any. But daughters go practiſe that little ſinne, Ile mend this great fault • re the fault begin. O couſening fortune how haſt thou deceiu'd me, Turning me out a doores to baniſhment, And made another Lord of Mantua. I that was Lord now ſlaue to miſery. VVhat things were thoſe? His reaſon for that? Man and wife part, thats ſtrange! VVhat ſhould we do? Stay forward daughters whether are yee going ▪ A wooing daughters? nere imagine ſo: What man's ſo mad to marry griefe and woe? But they are poore, and pouerty is deſpiſde: They once were faire, ſorrow from that hath changd them They once knew wealth, but chance hath much eſtrangd them, Come daughters, and come ſhepheards, if you pleaſe, Ile leade you to the lodge of little eaſe, Where I will feaſt you with what cheere I may, Griefe ſhall turne mirth, and keepe high holliday. You new-create me, and breath ſecond life Into my dying boſome, knew my ſoone Of this vnlookt-for Fortune, but ill Fate Has playd the Traytor, and giuen vp his life To coward treaſon.
Take comfort yet deare father. All diſcontent like to a wounded lyon He forrages the woods, daring proude fortune At her beſt weapon, he accounts this ſmart, As a ſlight hurt, but far off from the hart. Brother. Then ſince all dreame, let vs dreame of reuenge. Say ſiſter, had we not fine ſport to day? VVhy tis accounted pleaſure to kill fiſh. Yet fiſhes were created to be kild. Their bodies being food, maintaine our breath. Come, come, you vainely argue, it is good. If it be ſin, then you your ſelf's a ſinner. Shepheards or be what els you are well met. VVhat ere we ſaw ▪ you • et ere you came hither. So brothers without our leaues you well may be. Yet honeſt ſhepheard has with honeſt trade ſome ſtrife. So honeſt men do too aſwell as he. Sweare not, for we are misbeleeuers both. Oh time, ſometime ſhepheards haue idle howers. O heauen, how they can flatters to our faces. Exeunt. How now faire ſiſter? you are hard beſet. No, ſhepheards, now fiſh do not bite but play. My father, ſir, will chide if I be miſſing. Father, I thinke theſe ſhepheards come a wooing. Come brother, talke not of deuouring war, Say meſſenger, comes not Octauioes ſonnes? Then feare not father, my ſiſter and my ſelfe, Will be your champions and defend the Citty. Stand proud Franciſco. I will, but firſt Franciſco take my ſhielde. Read the conditions and returne your anſwers.
speeches.Ant: Comfort? no: My breſt's turnd priſon, my proude iaylor woe, Locks out all comfort: whers your valiant brother?
How holds his humour? Fitly applide for a walks like a ghoſt ▪ Why how now ſonne? Thou forgetteſt thy ſelfe. Prithee what wedding? I ſcarce beleeue that. That was miraculous! did they liue together? His wife and he liued together. How can he dreame, that neuer ſleeps my ſonne ▪ Pretty content; we kill our foes in dreames. Aſpero. Heare me. As many bleſſings as the ſea hath ſands Attend thee in thine honorable iourney: Come pretty maides we haue not wrought to day, Or fiſh, or faſt, our neede muſt needs obey. Early ſorrow, art got vp ſo ſoone? What? ere the Sun aſcendeth in the Eaſt? O what an early waker art thou growne? But ceaſe diſcourſe, and cloſe vnto thy worke; Vnder this drooping mirtle will I ſit, And worke a while vpon my corded net; And as I worke, record my ſorrowes paſt, Asking old Time, how long my woes ſhall laſt: And firſt, but ſtay alas what do J ſee? Moiſt gum like teares, drop from this mournfull tree And ſee, it ſticks like birdlyme; twill not part; Sorrow is euen ſuch birdlyme at my hart. Alas poore tree, doſt thou want company? Thou doſt, I ſee't, and J will weepe with thee, Thy ſorrowes make thee dumb, and ſo ſhall mine. It ſhall be tongueles, and ſo ſeeme like thine; Thus will I reſt my head vnto thy barke, Whilſt my ſighes tell my ſorrowes; harke tree, harke. Dales for Endimion and faire Cynthia fit, But neuer heauenly goddeſſe bleſt this groue, Theſe woods are conſecrate to griefe, not loue. Now truly ſhepheard none ſuch ſoiourn here Pleaſe you ſuruey the Cell, go in and ſee, I'me hearſt, and none but ſorrowe lies with me. Sons of Octanio if your princely thoughts Can ſtoope to ſuch meane beauty, from this hand Receiue your wiues, but ſhould the Duke your father— You that in all my baniſht pilgrimage, Would neuer alienate your naturall loues, But in deſire to ſee me reinſtalld, Haue thruſt out proude Octauices ſubſtitute, And ſeated me in antient dignity, I am yours, and ready at your beſt diſpoſe. The veynes and arteries of Anthonio Through which the bloud of greatneſſe flows in vs. Our life, and cauſe efficient of our ſtate, And theſe our prety partners in exile. Welcome thou hope of Mantua and of vs, VVe now are honors new beginners boy, And may we better thriue then heretofore. VVhat Lady's that. Octauioes daughter? The better welcome, I loue her for't. And Lady, though your Father be our foe, The vertuous loue betwixt our ſonne and you, May neretheleſſe retaine his ſimpathie.
The ſame faſhion ſtill: But ſomwhat •• dder-colourd death may end But neuer change him, ſee our words haue raiſd him. VVhat a ſleepe? A pleaſure nothing pleaſant to the fiſh. Cruell creation then to haue liues ſpild. What bodies then haue we to liue by death? What is it good to kill? oh god oh god? I thank proud fortune fort, my woes beginner. If not to vs you are vnto your ſelues. So ſhepheards we did meet for we are ſiſters. Know we deſire no husbands ſuch as you ▪ No neuer, if his oath be that he loues. Firſt we intreat you giue vs time to proue you. Good, if it had bin ſpoke behind our backs. Early ith' morning, or els late at night. Hold Hippolito. And mine as challenge to a ſingle combat,
Peace. Good now peace, VVake me not as you loue me. I, in a moſt ſweet ſleepe, bliſters o'your tongues for wa king me. J ſhould not be a Courtierels, mee thought J was at a ſtrange wedding? Of a young Lawyer and old Madam Conſcience. Nor J neither, becauſe it was a dreame, but mee thought the yong man doted on the old woman exceedingly. In the country they did, and agreed paſſing well, all the long vacation, and but for two things he would haue carried her vp to the • erme with him. One was, becauſe her gowne was of the old faſhion, the other was cauſe he would not haue her by when he tooke fees ▪ For feare if a bribe had bin offered, ſhe being by he ſhold haue had the bad conſcience to take it. Conſcience and the Lawyer, as louingly as men and their wiues do, one fleſh but neither medle nor make one with another O lord ſit, profit can part the ſoule and the body, and why not man and wife, now you haue had my dreame father, let me vnderſtand yours. O beſt of all: why, your whole world doth nothing but dreame, your machiauell he dreames of ſtate, depoſing kings, grounding new monarchies: the louer hee dreames of kiſſes, amorous embraces: the newe-married wife dreames, that rid of her young husband ſhe hugs her old loue, and likes her dreame well ynough too: the Country gentle woman dreams that when her firſt husband's dead, ſhe marries a knight, and the name of Lady ſticks ſo in her mind, that ſhees neuer at hearts eaſe till ſhe get her husband dub'd; the Captaine, he dreames of oppreſſing the ſouldiers, deuiſing ſtratage ̄ s, to keep his dreame, and that dreame wakes in the pate of Octauio your Arch-enemy ▪ who is not content to hurle vs into the whirlepoole of baniſh ment, but binds waights at our heeles leaden pouerty, to ſinke vs to the very depth that we ſhould neuer riſe againe. I marry ſiſter, that were a dreame worth dreaming, and ile ſleepe out my braines but ile compaſſe it. Vds foot, ile doe it waking then. At Counſell table. In his Dutches armes, twere baſe to go diſguiſd, No, my reuenge ſhall weare an open brow; J will not play the coward, kill him firſt And ſend my challenge after; ile make knowne My name, and cauſe of comming, if I thought Griefe like a painter had ſo ſpoyl'd mmy viſage He could not know me, on my breaſt ide write How ere I am diſfigured through woe, J am the thing was made for Aſpero. And you be not fitted in Venice tis ſtraunge, for tis counted the beſt fleſh ſhambles in Italie: but heer's no notable coward, that hauing ſuffered wrong by a man, ſeeks to right himſelfe of a woman. More then hir death, J haue bin in hir boſome ſir, and this day ſhe intends your execution. Hir humour, nothing but a kind of ſtrange croſſe humor in that you reiected hir loue. Not to croſſe a great ones humour? no treaſon more ▪ great perſonages humours are puritanes, thei'l as liue indure the diuel as ſoone as a croſſe, and can away with him better. Is your proud humour come down ifaith, your high humor that would not ſtoop an ynch of the knees; ile help't vp againe, and't be but to vphold the ieaſt; I muſt bring her as low ere I haue done; O baſe, J woulde rather lay my necke vnder the Axe of her hate, then my ſporte vnder the feete of hir humor; but be counſelld, ile teach you to preuent both, & per chance make her vpſtart humor ſtoope gallant too. And pawne me as poore Lords do their iewells too, will you not? receiue me; you ſhall counterfet your ſelfe dead. It may be ſhe diſſembles all this while, loues you, and puts on this ſhew of hate of purpoſe to humble you: ſhe may, and I beleeue— That moſt intelligencers are knaues, and ſome women diſ ſe ̄ blers; being thought dead (as let me alone to buz that into the credulous eare of the Court) if ſhe haue any ſparkes of loue, theil kindle and flame bright through the cinders of her hart. If not, twill be a meanes for your eſcape: ile ſay you reque ſted at your death to be buried at your natiue Citty: and what Courtier, if a Chriſtian can deny that? And if I do not kill it, I am not worthy to be your phyſitian. Well madam he. Very well. VVhere none of your proude ſex will euer come, I thinke: in heauen. See madam, and ſeeing bluſh, and bluſhing ſhame, that your vngentle humor ſhould be the death of ſo good and gene rous a ſpirit. Look to your • elfe my Lord, I lay my life, my Lady means to ſteale you away to night. Vdſfoot breake priſon my Lorde, tis but ſwimming the Riuer. Ile looke for my Fee then. Thats an exception Lawyers neuer reſpect, but come my lord, leape, as we haue riſen togither, weele fall togither, Yes faith, there had bin a Counſellors fee caſt away now. My Lord, your keeper hath brought a Lady or two to ſee you. Here. Here. J am ready for you ſir; O for a bul-ruſh to run a tilt at's noſe. O ſtrange, cannot you get vp without helpe? there's my gloue, but come no neerer, as you loue me. Oh blind loue. Not till they be nyne daies old my Lord, And the whole body to pleaſure you my Lord, but let me go a little. But you ſhall my Lord; hiſt, then keepe me ſtill. He faſtens the gloue to a poſt.

speeches.Pa. [Aspero's Boy]: My Lady cannot chooſe but dance well, ſhees ſo full of pre ty changes. Jt beares no relliſh of diſloyaltie: being in priſon you liue as far from loue as liberty: being abroad, you may by letters, or a thouſand meanes purchaſe hir company, and compaſſe your content.
You ſhall know him by theſe ſignes. A proper man without a beard. Faire ſpoken and well conditioned. Or your ſignet. Is he mad my Lord? If for light. I warne you my Lord, let mee alone, and we knew not how to abuſe a priſoner, we were not worthy to be a Iaylor. How now? who calls? You, what you? Foole, and ſo I leaue you. Foole, you lye, you are Aſpero, and I haue charge to keepe you in. From my Lord Hortenſio. 'Twill not ſerue your turne, J like a whole ſkinne better then a pinkt one: content your ſelfe to night, and in the morning ile tell you more. Shee's buſie with my Lord Hortenſio, but if you haue any vſe for a woman, ile ſend you one of the Laundreſſes: fare you well ſir, bee content, you ſhall want nothing of any thing you haue. O for a reaſonable audience to applaud this ſceane of mer ryment: ile goe call my Lady and my Lord Hortenſio. Hee's ſure ynough my Lord, he was a mad kn • ue when he came in, but J thinke, I haue made a t • me ſoole of him by this time: for a has neither had bread nor water theſe foure and forty houres. My Lord, Hortenſio was the villain, he left ſuch command with mee, hee's the wheele that turnes about, and I a Country Iack muſt ſtrike when I am commanded. Goblins, ſpirits, furie • , f • eryes, the priſon is haunted. Yes, and an olde foole my Lord, in the likeneſſe of Hortenſio. I know not my Lord: I let him in and my Lady to laugh at him, and it ſeemes, he conſented to treaſon, and let him out in his apparrell. It ſhall be done my Lord.
